Active Transport. It is the cellular process that moves molecules across the cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from low to high concentration, using energy from ATP hydrolysis. This mechanism allows cells to maintain essential ion gradients and accumulate vital nutrients despite thermodynamic resistance, and it is fundamental to neuronal signaling, muscle contraction, nutrient uptake, and the maintenance of cellular osmotic balance.

Active transport requires ATP hydrolysis to break chemical bonds and fuel conformational changes in transport proteins. The sodium-potassium pump, also known as the Na-plus, K-minus ATPase, is the most abundant cellular protein. It pumps three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP consumed. This creates and maintains membrane potential in neurons by establishing the sodium-potassium gradient that is critical for action potentials.

There are two main types. Primary active transport uses ATP directly, while secondary active transport harnesses the energy from another molecule's gradient, coupling the unfavorable uphill movement to a favorable downhill process. Active transport also enables the accumulation of calcium ions in mitochondria, triggering muscle contraction and intracellular signaling cascades. It powers the uptake of glucose and amino acids by intestinal and kidney cells against their concentration gradients.

The energy cost is significant. Active transport uses approximately thirty percent of cellular ATP at rest due to the sodium-potassium pump alone; disruption causes cell swelling and death. Transport proteins undergo conformational cycles: they bind substrate, hydrolyze ATP, change shape to release substrate on the opposite side, then reset to accept more incoming substrate molecules. Active transport proteins are themselves enzymes, coupling ATP hydrolysis to molecular movement, and they overcame the selectively permeable cell membrane through embedded pump proteins.
